title: Why silver tarnishes and how to slow it down
description: Silver tarnishes when it reacts with sulphur in the air. See what speeds it up in Indian homes, from monsoon damp to perfume, and easy habits that slow it.
keywords: how to stop silver from tarnishing
intro: Silver tarnishes because it reacts with sulphur compounds in the air, forming a thin dark layer of silver sulphide on the surface. You cannot stop it completely, because those compounds are everywhere, but you can slow it down a lot by keeping silver dry, away from certain chemicals and stored with little air around it.

sections.heading: What is actually happening to the metal
paragraphs: The air around us carries tiny amounts of sulphur-containing gases, such as hydrogen sulphide. They come from cooking, vehicle exhaust, rubber, some fabrics and even natural decay. When these gases meet silver, they react with the surface and leave behind silver sulphide, which looks yellow at first, then brown, then nearly black.

Sterling silver, with its 7.5% copper, can also show some copper oxidation, which is part of why sterling tarnishes a little faster than fine 999 silver. The good news is that tarnish sits on the surface. Underneath, the silver is fine, and a gentle clean brings back the shine.

sections.heading: Reading the colour: how far has tarnish gone?
paragraphs: It helps to recognise the stages, because early tarnish is far easier to remove.
list: Slight yellow or champagne tint: very early. A quick wipe with a silver polishing cloth is enough.
Patchy brown or rainbow-like sheen: moderate. A mild soap wash followed by a polishing cloth usually works.
Grey to black, especially in grooves: heavy. This may need a deeper clean, done carefully if the piece has stones or plating.
Black only in the recesses while raised areas stay bright: this is often a deliberate oxidised finish, not neglect. Do not try to remove it.

sections.heading: Everyday things that speed tarnish up
paragraphs: Humidity is the biggest one for Indian homes. During the monsoon, or if you live in a coastal city, moisture in the air helps the reaction along, and many people notice their silver darkening faster from June to September.

Your own routine matters too. Sweat, body lotion, sunscreen, perfume, deodorant and hair spray all leave residues on jewellery. Swimming pool chlorine is harsh on silver. Rubber bands, some foam packaging, wool and felt can release sulphur compounds, so storing silver wrapped in a rubber band or in an old felt box can actually make things worse.
In the kitchen, eggs, onions, mustard and some pickles give off sulphur as well. If you wear a silver ring or bracelet while cooking, it is likely to darken sooner.

sections.heading: Habits that slow tarnish down
paragraphs: None of these takes more than a few seconds, and together they make a visible difference.
list: Put jewellery on last, after perfume, lotion and makeup have dried.
Take it off before a bath, a swim, the gym or cooking.
Wipe each piece with a soft dry cloth before putting it away, to remove sweat and oils.
Store pieces in a small zip-lock pouch with the air pressed out, one piece per pouch so they do not scratch.
Add a silica gel sachet or an anti-tarnish strip to your jewellery box, and replace it every few months.
Keep silver out of the bathroom, where steam and humidity are highest.

sections.heading: Does wearing silver often help?
paragraphs: Many people find that a pendant worn every day stays brighter than one locked away, and there is a practical reason. Gentle friction from skin and clothes keeps polishing the surface, so tarnish does not get a chance to build up. A piece left in a damp drawer for months, on the other hand, often comes out much darker.
This works only if you also remove it for showers and workouts. Daily wear plus daily soap and sweat can leave a dull film that looks a lot like tarnish.

sections.heading: What about plated and rhodium-finished silver?
paragraphs: Many sterling pieces are finished with rhodium, a bright white metal that resists tarnish well, or with gold plating. These layers protect the silver underneath for as long as they last. Treat them gently: avoid harsh dips and abrasive polishes, which can wear the coating away and expose silver that will then tarnish unevenly.

If you are choosing a new pendant and want one that needs very little upkeep, check the listing for the finish. Varaha's [silver pendants](/silver) mention their plating on the product page, so you know what kind of care to expect before you buy.

faq.q: Is tarnish a sign of fake silver?
faq.a: No, the opposite. Real silver tarnishes because it reacts with sulphur in the air. Many fake pieces corrode differently or change colour where plating wears off.

faq.q: Why does my silver tarnish so fast in the monsoon?
faq.a: Moisture in the air speeds up the reaction between silver and sulphur compounds. Store pieces airtight with silica gel during humid months.
Surface tarnish can be cleaned off. Very heavy, long-neglected tarnish in fine detail can be harder to remove, so it is best dealt with early.

faq.q: Does rhodium plating stop silver tarnishing?
faq.a: It slows it a lot while the plating lasts. Once the rhodium wears thin, the silver below can start tarnishing again.
